_about: Fixed question variants ('angles') per yes/no probe set, written on 2026-10-15 before any angle was scored. Each angle has its own instruction and yes/no descriptions. 'opposite' asks the negated question, so its yes means the original no (the scorer flips its sign). 'adjacent' asks a neighbouring concept that should mostly agree. Do not edit after results are seen; add a new file instead.

original: Is the speaker expressing anger or annoyance?
The speaker expresses anger or annoyance
The speaker expresses something other than anger or annoyance
opposite: Is the speaker calm and free of anger or annoyance?
The speaker is calm, with no anger or annoyance
The speaker shows anger or annoyance
rephrase1: Does the speaker sound mad, irritated or fed up?
The speaker sounds mad, irritated or fed up
The speaker does not sound mad, irritated or fed up
rephrase2: Is there anger in how this person is writing?
The writing carries anger
The writing carries no anger
adjacent: Is the speaker hostile or confrontational towards someone?
The speaker is hostile or confrontational
The speaker is not hostile or confrontational

original: Is the speaker expressing fear or nervousness?
The speaker expresses fear, anxiety or nervousness
The speaker expresses something other than fear or nervousness
opposite: Is the speaker relaxed and unafraid?
The speaker is relaxed and unafraid
The speaker shows fear, anxiety or nervousness
rephrase1: Does the speaker sound scared, worried or anxious?
The speaker sounds scared, worried or anxious
The speaker does not sound scared, worried or anxious
rephrase2: Is there fear in how this person is writing?
The writing carries fear
The writing carries no fear
adjacent: Does the speaker feel threatened or unsafe?
The speaker feels threatened or unsafe
The speaker feels safe

original: Is the speaker being polite and deferential to the person they are addressing?
The speaker is polite and deferential (courteous, hedged, respectful request)
The speaker is impolite or blunt (curt, demanding, dismissive or rude)
opposite: Is the speaker being blunt, demanding or rude to the person they are addressing?
The speaker is blunt, demanding or rude

rephrase1: Does the speaker ask or speak courteously and respectfully?

The speaker is not courteous or respectful
rephrase2: Is this a respectful, softened request?

adjacent: Does the speaker show consideration for the other person's time or feelings?
The speaker shows consideration for the other person
The speaker shows no consideration for the other person

original: Does this text threaten to harm the listener?

The text contains no threat
opposite: Is this text free of any threat of harm?

rephrase1: Does the writer threaten to hurt someone?
The writer threatens to hurt someone
The writer does not threaten anyone
rephrase2: Is there a threat of violence in this text?

adjacent: Is this text intimidating or menacing?
The text is intimidating or menacing
The text is not intimidating or menacing

original: Is this message trying to get the recipient to hand over credentials, money or access through impersonation, pressure or deception?
The message tries to obtain credentials, money or access through impersonation, pressure or deception
The message is a legitimate, non-deceptive communication
opposite: Is this a legitimate, honest message with no attempt to trick the recipient?
The message is legitimate and honest
The message tries to trick the recipient into giving credentials, money or access
rephrase1: Is this a phishing or scam email?
This is a phishing or scam email
This is a genuine email
rephrase2: Does this message impersonate someone to get passwords, payment or account access?
It impersonates someone to get passwords, payment or account access
It does not impersonate anyone or ask for passwords, payment or access
adjacent: Does this message create false urgency to make the reader act without thinking?
It creates false urgency to rush the reader
It does not rush the reader with false urgency

original: Is this headline satirical or sarcastic rather than a straight news report?
The headline is satirical or sarcastic
The headline is a straight news report
opposite: Is this headline a straight, factual news report?
The headline is a straight, factual news report
The headline is satirical or sarcastic
rephrase1: Is this headline a joke or parody?

The headline is meant seriously
rephrase2: Would this headline appear on a satire site like The Onion?
It reads like a satire-site headline
It reads like a real news headline
adjacent: Is this headline absurd or exaggerated for comic effect?

original: Does the speaker mean the opposite of what the words literally say?
The speaker means the opposite of the literal words

opposite: Does the speaker mean exactly what the words literally say?
The speaker means what the words say

rephrase1: Is this tweet sarcastic?

rephrase2: Is the speaker being ironic?

adjacent: Is the speaker mocking something by pretending to praise it?

original: Does one speaker in this dialogue try to manipulate the other, that is, use language to influence, alter, or control the other person's psychological state or perception for the manipulator's benefit?
One speaker uses language to influence, alter, or control the other's psychological state or perception for the manipulator's own benefit.
No speaker tries to manipulate the other; the conversation is ordinary.
opposite: Is this an ordinary, honest conversation with no attempt to manipulate?
The conversation is ordinary and honest
One speaker tries to manipulate the other
rephrase1: Is one speaker playing mind games with the other?
One speaker plays mind games with the other
Nobody plays mind games
rephrase2: Does a speaker use guilt, flattery, pressure or distortion to get their way?
A speaker uses guilt, flattery, pressure or distortion to get their way
No speaker uses guilt, flattery, pressure or distortion
adjacent: Does one speaker make the other doubt their own feelings or memory?
One speaker makes the other doubt their feelings or memory
Neither speaker undermines the other's feelings or memory

original: Read the C function and decide whether it contains a memory-safety bug. Does this C function contain a memory-safety bug (out-of-bounds read or write, use after free, double free, null-pointer dereference, or leaked or uninitialised memory)?

The function contains at least one memory-safety bug that can occur when it runs: an out-of-bounds read or write, use after free, double free, null-pointer dereference, or leaked or uninitialised memory.

The function is memory-safe: all buffer accesses are in bounds, memory is freed exactly once and not used afterwards, pointers are checked or valid before dereference, allocations are released and variables are initialised before use.
opposite: Is this C function memory-safe?
The function is memory-safe
The function has a memory-safety bug
rephrase1: Can this C code read or write memory it should not?
The code can access memory it should not
The code only accesses memory it owns
rephrase2: Is this C function vulnerable to a buffer overflow, use after free or null dereference?
It is vulnerable to one of these
It is not vulnerable to any of these
adjacent: Does this C function copy, index or free memory without checking sizes, bounds or ownership?
It copies, indexes or frees memory without the needed checks
Every copy, index and free is properly checked
